ex.4: Convergency = Δlong × sin mean lat, so the pair with the highest mean latitude (60°N/55°N) gives the biggest difference.
ex.5: Conversion angle = ½ × Δlong × sin mean lat = 5 × sin 54.5° ≈ 4°. In the northern hemisphere the great circle lies poleward of the rhumb line, so RL = 100 + 4 = 104°T.
ex.9: South 360 NM → 54°N. East 360 NM at 54°N = 612' of longitude; west 360 NM at 60°N = 720'. Net 108' ≈ 1° 48' west → 031° 48'W.
ex.14: The printed question says 'a TAS of > 150 kt', which makes none of the options right; the source question reads 'less than 150 kt'. TAS below RAS means the air is denser than ISA sea level.
ex.22: The book uses the runway number (060°): angle 40°, so 20 / sin 40° ≈ 31 kt. (With QDM 063°, 20 / sin 37° ≈ 33 kt.)
ex.24: Wind 50° off the nose from the left: drift ≈ 6°, GS ≈ 450 cos 6° − 60 cos 50° ≈ 409 kt. 315 / 409 ≈ 46 min → 0736.
ex.34: 29 000 ft at 1800 ft/min = 16.1 min, covering 16.1/60 × 200 ≈ 54 NM. Cruise 165 − 54 = 111 NM at 350 kt = 19 min → start descent at 0449.
ex.35: The book treats 62 050 kg as the limiting zero fuel mass: traffic load = 62 050 − 40 970 = 21 080 kg (TOM 89 200 would allow 21 370 kg).
ex.38: Take-off fuel = tank 16 100 − taxi 200 = 15 900 kg. Traffic = 66 200 − 33 500 − 15 900 = 16 800 kg.
ex.44: 070°W and 110°E are on the same great circle through the pole: (90 − 56) + (90 − 62) = 62° × 60 = 3720 NM.
ex.45: Same latitude, 75° further west = 5 h later: 0243 + 0500 = 0743 UTC.
ex.48: The error is 4°. By the 1 in 60 rule, 200 NM × 4/60 ≈ 13–14 NM off track.
ex.53: ROD ≈ GS × 101 × tan 3° ≈ 100 × 101 × 0.052 ≈ 530 ft/min, i.e. about −500 ft/min.
ex.79: Flying 090°T towards the VOR, the aircraft is due west of it: true bearing from the station 270°. Use the variation at the station: 270 − 15 = 255°.
ex.80: The aircraft is due south of the VOR: 180°T − 13°E = 167°.
ex.83: Book key prints (c). Ionospheric (D-layer) absorption is lowest at night and decreases as frequency increases, so the correct answer is (a) midnight and high frequency.
ex.96: Book key prints (b). The date line roughly follows the 180° meridian, and travelling westwards across it you move into the next day (for example, leaving Los Angeles on Monday you arrive in Tokyo on Tuesday).
